title: Telecom stocks: how to analyze telecom and media companies
description: Telecom stocks are analyzed on capital and subscribers: ARPU, churn, capex, net debt/EBITDA — the method with worked examples and sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Telecom stocks are shares in companies that build and run communications networks — and, in the wider sense, the media companies filling them with content and services. The span runs from operators like Telia, Tele2, Deutsche Telekom and Telenor via streaming services like Netflix and Spotify to advertising platforms like Meta. The common denominator is the subscription: revenues are recurring, measurable per subscriber and predictable month by month. The question is rarely whether revenue arrives, but what it costs to build, acquire and keep.

This guide walks through both halves — network and content capital economics — via the ratios that hold them together: ARPU, churn, capex share and net debt per EBITDA, with worked examples and sources.

## The industry's two halves — networks and content

The industry splits into two capital logics. The operator owns physical infrastructure: towers, fiber, radio equipment and — via licenses — spectrum rights. The media company owns content and audience relationships: film, music and sport rights, platforms gathering attention. Platform companies are a third variant: users create the content and [network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter) make the service more valuable for each new participant.

The scale is striking: mobile technologies and services generated 7.6 trillion dollars in 2025 — 6.4 percent of world GDP (GSMA). But the economics split at the investment decision: the operator ties up capital in networks depreciated over decades, the media company in content that becomes a catalog or a written-off loss — same subscription, different balance sheets.

## Telecom stocks in practice — spectrum, capex and debt

The operator's key raw material is spectrum, allocated at auction. When the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority (PTS) held its 5G auction in the 3.5 and 2.3 GHz bands, SEK 2.3 billion was raised in one auction day — Telia paid SEK 760 million for 120 megahertz. The 2023 auction in the 900, 2100 and 2600 MHz bands brought a further SEK 4.2 billion. Licenses run on time: capital is tied up, depreciated, renewed — a structural clock like the patent in pharma.

The buildout comes on top: towers, radio, fiber. Capex — new investments — normally sits around 15–20 percent of revenues at mature operators, separating telecom from most industries: the result after depreciation rarely looks like the cash flow. Depreciation is a judgment call, making [the EBITDA margin](/blogg/v08-ebitda-marginal-analys) and [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) — not the income statement — the primary reading.

Debt is the third leg: builds and spectrum buys are one-off costs usually financed with loans, which is why operators are measured on net debt per EBITDA rather than the debt-to-equity ratio. [How to calculate EV/EBITDA](/blogg/sa-raknar-du-ev-ebitda) goes through the multiple that cleans out capital structure; [which debt level is dangerous](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig), the boundaries. The norm often sits around two to three years of EBITDA — read it against the investment cycle, never in isolation.

The growth story stands in the industry reports: 5G subscriptions have passed three billion and are expected to reach 6.4 billion by the end of 2031 (Ericsson Mobility Report). The question is who pays: each buildout must be covered by revenue per subscriber — otherwise it eats the dividend.

## ARPU and churn — the subscriber's economics

Both halves live on the same equation: paying subscribers times revenue per subscriber — ARPU. Worked example: SEK 150 per month is SEK 1,800 per year and subscriber. Acquisition and retention are the real growth lines.

Churn — the share leaving per period — decides the relationship's length. A monthly churn of 1.5 percent means an average relationship of 1 ÷ 0.015 ≈ 67 months, just over five and a half years — roughly SEK 10,000 per subscriber. Set that against the acquisition cost — discounts, subsidies, marketing: high churn makes acquisition recurring, low churn a one-off on a long revenue string. ARPU trend and churn are read together: falling ARPU at an unchanged subscriber count is an invisible decline — same base, lower revenue per subscriber.

## The media company — subscribers, content and operating leverage

The media side has the same top line but a different cost base. Netflix reported over 325 million paying households in the fourth quarter of 2025 and forecasts 2026 revenue of 50.7–51.7 billion dollars; Spotify reached 761 million monthly users, 293 million paying, in the first quarter of 2026. Revenue is still subscribers times price — and the content cost is the medium's capex: the production and rights budget, the operator network's counterpart.

The difference: content is depreciated on popularity, not on time. A library's booked value is a set of assumptions about audience taste; when they miss, write-downs arrive. The Swedish example is Viaplay, which after expansive sports rights purchases had to rework its content commitments in 2023 — content deals are obligations. The medium's accounts are read in two lines: the subscriber trend and the character of the content cost — fixed, variable or binding.

Operating leverage ties it together: the content budget is essentially fixed, the cost of streaming to one more viewer near zero — every subscriber beyond break-even is almost pure margin; mirror-wise, fixed costs strike just as hard when subscribers leave. Scalability is profit and loss in one package; growth against capital burn is read through [Capital burn](/kurser/v19-kapitalforbranning), subscription revenue's measures in [ARR growth](/kurser/v02-arr-tillvaxt) and [what accessible revenues say](/blogg/arr-tillvaxt-vad-atkommande-intakter-sager).

## The worked example — the operator's cash flow

Put numbers on an invented operator. Revenue SEK 30 billion; EBITDA SEK 12 billion — a margin of 40 percent, normal for a mature network. Capex SEK 6 billion, that is 20 percent of revenue. Cash flow before interest and tax: 12 − 6 = SEK 6 billion; after interest of SEK 1.2 billion, SEK 4.8 billion remains for dividends, amortization and the next buildout. Net debt is SEK 30 billion — 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5× EBITDA.

Note the reading order: [EV/EBITDA](/kurser/km-010-evebit) first, then capex share, then debt — P/E last, since depreciation judgments make the denominator unsteady. The dividend space is what remains when everything obligatory is paid: [the dividend yield](/kurser/km-063-direktavkastning) counts on free cash flow, not reported earnings.

## The regulation — the authority in the equation

The operator is one of the exchange's most regulated businesses. In Sweden PTS supervises under the Electronic Communications Act (2022:482) — the statute whose cookie rules you meet on every website. Regulation sets the rules: spectrum access, interconnection, number portability, consumer protection. Authority decisions are a catalyst class of their own — an auction changes the capital binding, a rulebook a revenue model — systematized in [Regulatory catalysts](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska).

## Three pitfalls

- **A low P/E as a value trap.** A mature operator can trade at a low multiple and still be expensive if the buildout cycle eats cash flow for years. The multiple is the question; the capex share is the answer.
- **The subscription is not eternal.** Subscription revenues are stable, not sacred: price competition, churn and technology shifts — landline to mobile, copper to fiber — can rewrite a revenue base silently.
- **The content's value is an estimate.** A media company's library is booked at assumptions about audience taste; booked value says nothing about future viewing time — read the subscriber base and the content commitments instead.

## The summary

- Telecom stocks and media companies live on the same equation: subscribers × ARPU; churn decides the length of the relationship — 67 months at 1.5 percent per month in the example.
- The operator is read on EBITDA, capex share (normally 15–20 percent of revenue) and net debt per EBITDA (often 2–3×); the income statement is governed by depreciation judgments.
- Spectrum auctions tie up capital on time — the Swedish PTS 5G auctions raised SEK 2.3 and 4.2 billion.
- The medium's capex is the content: depreciated on popularity, with operating leverage as a double-acting mechanism.
- A low P/E is always read with capex and debt beside it.
